title: Students squeezed out of university courses after bumper A-level grades
summary:
Students narrowly missing grades are being rejected, while some on oversubscribed courses are asked to defer

Students across the UK have found themselves unexpectedly squeezed out of their desired university courses as this year’s bumper crop of A-level grades ​h​as not always translated into ​​the places many were hoping for.

​With close to a third of the A-levels awarded in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving the top A and A* grades this year, universities are taking a tougher stance by rejecting students who narrowly missed their expected grades and who in previous years would still have gained a place.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Students across the UK have found themselves unexpectedly squeezed out of their desired university courses as this year’s bumper crop of A-level grades ​h​as not always translated into ​​the places many were hoping for.

​With close to a third of the A-levels awarded in England, Wales and Northern Ireland achieving the top A and A* grades this year, universities are taking a tougher stance by rejecting students who narrowly missed their expected grades and who in previous years would still have gained a place.

The stronger competition has tipped record numbers of applicants into clearing, or settling for their second choices, with universities in some cases wanting students to defer for a year.

Cardiff ​University ​h​as asked students on two programmes to defer until 2027, after more than expected achieved their required grades, leaving it with a surplus of qualified applicants for courses such as midwifery.​

The university said it had asked “a small number” of applicants to defer, with limits on its intake previously agreed with the Welsh government.

“We understand this will be deeply disappointing for those affected, and our immediate priority is to support these students and ensure they receive clear guidance as they consider their next steps,” a spokesperson for Cardiff said.

“It is important to be clear that Cardiff University has not over-offered places. As with all universities, offers are made based on detailed modelling of applicant behaviour and historical acceptance patterns. This year, an exceptionally high number of applicants met the conditions of their offers and accepted places, resulting in demand exceeding the number of commissioned places available.

“This has been an extremely difficult decision … and we explored every possible option to avoid activating the university’s oversubscription policy for these two courses.”

At least one applicant said she had complained to the Office for Students, telling Wales Online that Cardiff had offered her a £750 bursary to defer or lose her place. The Office for Students does not regulate universities in Wales.

Ucas figures show that this year, 73% of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland were given firm offers after grades were issued, below the 76% with firm offers in 2024 and 2025. A record 23,000 students have already deferred their places this year.

Figures published on Friday show record numbers of students were eligible for clearing, the post-results process to apply for courses with unfilled places.

The proportion of applicants receiving their first-choice course offer was lower this year at 79%, compared with 82% last year, while the proportion placed at their “insurance” choice increased.

The competition for places has increased as a result of selective universities growing less slowly than last year, despite record numbers of applications. While selective universities received almost 10% more applications this year, the universities have only increased offers by 5% compared with 2025.

title: How 4 Colleges Are Supporting Student Parents
summary:
How 4 Colleges Are Supporting Student Parents
Joshua.Bay Fri, 08/14/2026 - 03:00 AM

From scholarships and free childcare to pre-orientation programs and workforce training, institutions are helping student parents and caregivers persist.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
For students who are also parents or caregivers, persisting to graduation can depend on whether colleges account for responsibilities that extend far beyond the classroom.

Recent initiatives tackle those barriers from several directions—from scholarships and free childcare to pre-orientation programs and workforce training.

Here are four institutions rethinking how they support the success of student parents and caregivers.

Generations College: Expanding College Access for Single Parents

Generations College in Illinois launched its Single Parent Scholarship program in 2020 after college leaders saw the cost of childcare becoming an increasingly common obstacle for student parents. The scholarship covers remaining tuition after grant aid, allowing recipients to earn an associate degree at no cost.

Available to full-time, Pell Grant–eligible students who are single parents, the program provides up to $3,500 per semester. To remain eligible, students must maintain a cumulative GPA of at least 2.5.

Demand has grown steadily since the program’s launch: This year alone, Generations College awarded nearly 90 scholarships.

Chancellor Grace Alexis said the institution serves a large share of adult learners, many of whom balance school, work and family responsibilities. More than half of the college’s student parents are raising their children on their own, and the scholarship has become one of the institution’s largest financial aid programs.

“We just wanted to provide them with a sense of hope that, ‘Yes, you too can still obtain your college degree, despite the fact that you have all of these other obligations,’” Alexis said. “It takes everything from the parent to make it work. They sacrifice themselves, their education [and] their lifestyle in order to provide food, shelter and the necessities for their children.”

Wichita State University: Building Belonging Before Classes Begin

Wichita State University in Kansas introduced the new Parents and Caregivers Community Program this fall as part of its annual Shocker Pre-Season programming, which offers pre-orientation experiences designed for specific student groups or about certain topics before the fall semester begins.

The online, asynchronous program is designed to help students who are parents or caregivers connect with peers in similar stages of life, explore family-friendly spaces on campus and learn about resources that can support their academic, social and mental well-being.

Brett Petersen-Bruner, associate vice provost for student success and persistence at Wichita State, said the pre-orientation program grew out of a virtual workshop for student parents hosted by the university’s Office of Online and Adult Learning in spring 2024.

He said two themes emerged: Student parents wanted intentional spaces to build community and belonging with others in similar situations, and many expressed feelings of parental guilt as they tried to balance academics with their other responsibilities.

“We really thought intentionally about ‘How do we onboard student parents in family-friendly ways?’” Petersen-Bruner said. “That has served over the last couple years as our motivation to really think about reimagining our support for students who are parents or caregivers.”

LaGuardia Community College: Removing Childcare Barriers to Persistence

LaGuardia Community College in New York offers Horizons NYC, a free seven-week summer program that combines childcare with academic enrichment, swimming, art and field trips. Now entering its second year, Horizons NYC at LaGuardia is the first and only Horizons program in New York City located on a college campus, serving student parents and their children.

The college’s Early Childhood Learning Center already provides free, year-round childcare for 209 children of student parents, ranging in age from 6 months to 12 years; Horizons NYC expands that support during the summer by serving additional children through its enrichment program.

Each summer, the program welcomes a new cohort of rising kindergartners, adding a grade level as returning students get older. This summer, the program reached capacity with 45 students—15 each entering in kindergarten, first and second grade—and has a wait list.

Sonya Evariste, executive director of the Early Childhood Learning Center programs at LaGuardia, said the Horizons wait list reflects the strong demand among student parents for affordable summer childcare. She noted that Horizons will continue expanding one grade each year until it serves students from kindergarten through ninth grade.

“We wanted to ensure that we have campus childcare available for student parents so that they can meet their goals and finish their education without worrying about their children,” Evariste said. “Having their children right here on campus is major for them.”

Marymount University: Turning Caregiving Skills Into Career Opportunities

Marymount University in Virginia offers the From Caregiver to Breadwinner program, which is based on the premise that caregiving develops skills employers value but often overlook.

The private Catholic university launched the workforce initiative in 2024 to help unpaid family caregivers transition into careers in information technology. Through the no-cost, 12-week program, participants receive training in IT and artificial intelligence fundamentals, prepare for industry-recognized certifications, including CompTIA Tech+, and receive mentorship, career coaching and job-placement support.

Established by the university’s Center for the Innovative Workforce, the program has served more than 140 participants so far.

Diane Murphy, director of the Center for the Innovative Workforce, said the idea for the program emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many parents—particularly women—left the workforce because of caregiving responsibilities. As technology reshaped the job market and employers sought new digital skills, many women found it difficult to return to work.

“We felt this was a needy population that nobody was really paying too much attention to,” Murphy said. “But if we’ve got a tech workforce crunch, they are people who already have good skills, particularly customer service skills, which are a little low in IT help desk work.”

For Maria Ghafoor, one of the program’s participants, that opportunity offered a path forward after years spent caring for her son, Momin. After he suffered a stroke at birth, she stepped away from her career as a medical assistant to become his full-time caregiver.

“I was completely at my lowest at that time because I was not focusing on myself as much as I was giving it all to my family, being the caregiver,” Ghafoor said. “This was the one hope that actually brought me forward.”

title: Troy Punishes Professor for Writing to Lawmakers on University Letterhead
summary:
Troy Punishes Professor for Writing to Lawmakers on University Letterhead
Emma Whitford Fri, 08/14/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
A Troy University professor who sent a personal letter to Alabama lawmakers received a disciplinary notice from his department chair, claiming he issued “unauthorized communication” on “behalf of Troy University” by using university letterhead, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression announced in a news release Thursday.

Micah Swartz, a math professor at Troy, wrote to Alabama legislative officials in April about his concerns with the Alabama Numeracy Act Course Review Committee, FIRE reported.

“I am writing … because my first year in this role has been the most challenging of my career—and not for any of the usual reasons. The workload, the service obligations, the research I am conducting, and the move away from family have all been manageable,” Swartz wrote. “What has not been manageable is the Alabama Numeracy Act (ANA) Course Review Committee’s handling of Troy University’s proposed undergraduate numeracy syllabi.”

His department chair wrote that using the university letterhead “represented he was communicating in an official capacity on behalf of Troy University,” according to FIRE. Swartz shared the letter with his students and later received a second disciplinary notice in May for “unprofessional conduct,” according to the release. FIRE is calling on the university to rescind the two disciplinary letters. Beyond the two notices, it’s unclear what disciplinary actions have been taken, if any.

“The right to petition government officials is one of the core expressive freedoms explicitly protected by the First Amendment. Academics don’t surrender that right just because they choose to work at a state school,” said Zach Greenberg, FIRE’s director of faculty legal defense. “By attempting to silence a professor for speaking out about how taxpayer dollars are being spent—and then punishing him again for sharing his plight with others—Troy is setting a chilling precedent that would lead to more censorship and less government accountability across the state of Alabama.”

Troy University declined to comment on the case, citing “confidential personnel matters.”

But in a statement to Inside Higher Ed, a university spokesperson wrote that Troy “respects the rights of faculty and staff to speak as private citizens on matters of public concern. Employees speaking in a personal capacity are expected to make clear that they do not represent the University and to ensure that their statements could not reasonably be perceived as an institutional endorsement.”

title: Accreditor Puts Lane Community College on Warning
summary:
Accreditor Puts Lane Community College on Warning
kathryn.palmer… Fri, 08/14/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
A regional accrediting agency has sanctioned Lane Community College over its ongoing governance issues.

Last week, the Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities sent LCC President Stephanie Bulger a letter notifying her that the college in Eugene, Ore., is now on accreditation warning. The NWCCU’s decision stems from a special review of the college it conducted in March in response to complaints that some trustees exhibited racist and sexist behavior toward Bulger, a Black woman, during multiple 2025 board meetings; a third-party report released last year supported those claims. The board censured the former board chair, and the full board also issued a joint apology.

The accreditor’s subsequent review found that the college failed to uphold requirements that it “demonstrate an effective governance structure” and exemplify “high ethical standards in its management and operations, including in its dealings with the public, NWCCU, and external organizations, including the fair and equitable treatment of students, faculty, administrators, staff, and other stakeholders and constituencies.”

The NWCCU has given LCC until Aug. 5, 2030, to “take appropriate action” and “show evidence” of effective, respectful governance that maintains “clearly defined authority, roles, and responsibilities.”

The NWCCU also told the college that it needs to improve “dealing with its stakeholders” and make sure it “adheres to clearly defined policies that prohibit conflicts of interest on the part of members of the governing board.”

In a joint statement on the sanctions, Bulger and Jesse Maldonado, chair of the LCC Board of Education, said they “take the findings seriously and accept the responsibility that comes with them,” according to KLCC, Eugene’s NPR affiliate. “We know that how the Board governs affects the campus beyond Board meetings. It shapes how decisions are made, how clearly roles are understood across the college, and how effectively the institution can respond to challenges.”

The NWCCU asked LCC to provide an update on its progress in fall 2027.

title: Average cost of a packed lunch for school now tops $6
summary: As the price of groceries rises, what once was an affordable option — cooking at home— has become more of a burden on families
full_text:
The average cost of a packed lunch for school has topped $6 as Americans struggle to afford everyday necessities.

The back-to-school season is always pricey for parents, with the cost of supplies, new clothes, and the superhero or princess backpack that your kid insisted on. The rising cost of groceries has added to that burden at a time when budgets are already tight.

The average daily cost of a packed lunch is now $6.33, up two percent from last year, according to the global accounting firm Deloitte.

"It feels like almost week to week that our groceries are becoming more expensive when we're not buying extra things," Alexandra Thompson, a 31-year-old from Union City, Tennessee, recently told USA TODAY. "There's no joy in living this way.”

The price of groceries rose 2.7 percent in July from the previous year, according to the Consumer Price Index, which the government uses to track the cost of goods and services over time.

While many school districts offer lunch served in the cafeteria for free, or at a reduced price, fewer children automatically qualify due to changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program made under the Trump administration.

Children from families that receive SNAP automatically qualify for free school meals.

As of July 21, more than one million children have lost SNAP benefits as a result of the changes, according to the Washington, D.C. think tank Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, making it harder for these kids to get free lunch.

If you plan to brown bag it, Jacque DeVille, a producer for Louisiana news outlet KSLA who spoke to a child nutrition expert, has listed some tips for cutting costs when preparing school lunches.

Parents should choose full-size items instead of individually packaged portions and, if you have room in the budget, buy pantry goods such as nut butters in bulk.

Batch cooking can also help busy parents in the morning; just try to switch up how you prepare the dish.

“One rotisserie chicken can stretch across several different lunch recipes throughout the week,” DeVille said. “So kids aren’t eating the same thing every day.”

title: Brooks and Atkins Stohr on 'woke' politics in America
summary: David Brooks of The Atlantic and Kimberly Atkins Stohr of the Boston Globe join William Brangham to discuss the week in politics, including the surprising result in Wisconsin's Democratic primary, the status of 'woke' politics in America and the stalemate between the U.S. and Iran.
full_text:
William Brangham:

To discuss the major upset in Wisconsin's Democratic primary this week, as well as the stalemate between the U.S. and Iran, and more, we turn to Brooks and Atkins Stohr. That's "The Atlantic"'s David Brooks and Kimberly Atkins Stohr of The Boston Globe. Jonathan Capehart is away.

Happy Friday. Welcome to you both.

David Brooks:

Thank you.

Kimberly Atkins Stohr, The Boston Globe:

Hi. Thanks.

William Brangham:

David, let's talk a little bit about what happened in Wisconsin.

The Democratic primary for governor there had this big upset, where David Crowley went into this race, in this election looking like he was going to get trounced. And he ekes out a win over Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong. Was this simply your sense that voters simply thought Hong is not a great candidate to run statewide, or was something else afoot?

David Brooks:

It's worth mentioning David Crowley dropped out of the race like a month ago.

William Brangham:

Right.

David Brooks:

He only reentered it a month ago.

William Brangham:

Right.

David Brooks:

So never give up, kids.

(Laughter)

David Brooks:

I -- people are saying, is this the end of the DSA moment?

William Brangham:

Democratic Socialists of America.

David Brooks:

The Democratic Socialists of America moment, the leftward surge. I think probably not.

I think Francesca Hong was a uniquely bad candidate, not only because of some positions she had that would be considered extreme by people like me, but because of all the personal stuff, all the stuff that was on Twitter during the woke era, and attacking Thanksgiving. She had a thing for holidays. Valentine's Day, she was against it, one after another, and they were bizarre, sometimes bizarre positions.

And then when she was asked during the campaign, she looked terrible on TV on those big TV interviews. And she couldn't just say, I have changed my mind, which is what she should have said. What Mamdani has said, that's what you should say. And so I don't think this is a big indictment of the socialists, though I wish it was. I think she was just a uniquely bad candidate that caused this polling collapse at the end.

William Brangham:

I mean, Kimberly, the Republicans clearly relished the idea of running against Hong, and now they don't have that as a as a foil in this election.

Again, do you think this is just pragmatism on their part, or, as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of the more famous of the socialists, Democratic socialists out there, recently said, the woke point 1.0 era is over, and I'm glad for it?

Kimberly Atkins Stohr:

Yes, so I think a couple things are at play here. I agree with you that candidates matter, and you have to have a good candidate running, and that will trump anything in a race.

I also think that gubernatorial races are precise things, that you can't always draw national implications out of them. I mean, a state like Massachusetts for many, many years had the -- blue as the sky, but loved elect Republican governors because they like those checks and balances. So they do like different ideologies for different positions.

I don't think that you can extrapolate on congressional races, for example, there. But I also think in terms of is woke 2.0 better than woke 1.0, I think what we are seeing and what voters are responding to are candidates that respond to the needs of the moment.

2020, there were different needs. We were in a pandemic. We were locked down. We were seeing police brutality right before us. We were seeing the Trump administration completely fall apart, and there was a different urgency there. Right now, the biggest urgency is economic.

And you are seeing people who are excelling where they can make voters understand, look, I understand that affordability is an issue for you, that housing affordability, that gas prices are rising, and I want to get into office to work for you. That message seems to be just on fire at this moment. And it's something that Republicans are having a really difficult time responding to.

William Brangham:

David, do you think that that's right, I mean, that, one, that it's all about where you are trying to run? Like, Mamdani is not going to win an election in Iowa. But do you believe what AOC was saying, that that era is over, as Kimberly is saying, and that the Democrats are responding to the moment appropriately?

David Brooks:

Well, I agree with her when she said it was crazy. I think it was a crazy period to live through. I think many, many hundreds of people lost their jobs because they said something that was supposedly offensive or had a thought that was supposedly offensive.

The range of public debate, especially on college campuses, was permanently chilled. We're still living with the effects of that, because students have, 70 or 80 percent, say, I don't feel I can say what I believe in public.

And, third, it elected Donald Trump. I mean, his devastating ad in 2024 was he's for you, she's for they/them.

William Brangham:

This was the trans issue.

David Brooks:

Yes. And it was an ad that -- a line that summarized the whole woke period and showed how some Democrats, especially privileged Democrats at highly competitive colleges, were way out of touch with America.

The period has slowed down, so people are much more free to have conversations which they were not four years ago. And the focus has shifted to economics. But the DSA still comes with some pretty extreme views. Should we eliminate the prison system? Should we completely open the borders? These are somewhat views that I don't think you could get elected, but a lot of people are willing to look past them in order to get the angriest Democrat who's out there, and those tend to be the DSA people.

William Brangham:

I mean, Kimberly, the -- some Democratic critics of the president say that, yes, the Republicans do like to fetish the woke era, but they argue you also have a Republican Party that is in virtual lockstep with Donald Trump.

And what they argue is his very open war on all of the democratic norms of our society, and that that is a much bigger liability. Do you think that that's true?

Kimberly Atkins Stohr:

I think multiple things can be true at once. That's certainly a big liability.

People -- Donald Trump's approval ratings on all the things he ran on, affordability, two to three down in the polls. Immigration, more than half of Americans are disagreeing with his policies and the way that immigration policy is going. So you have that.

But at the same time, to push back against your point about how what a disaster woke 1.0 was, we are seeing the results of what people were talking about then. We are seeing a work force where the federal work force is -- was decimated, including Black women disproportionately hit. You are seeing Republicans vilify trans people and LGBTQ people with zest and zeal.

You are seeing DEI, whatever they call DEI, being eliminated in a way that even the president is putting up signs on Smithsonian saying that it's a lie if it talks about the plight of Black or brown Americans, which is factual. You're seeing such a backlash against all of those things, which is in part because Democrats were walking away from it.

I think Democrats have to build a big tent that focuses on all of the things that are happening as a result of the Trump administration, both economically and otherwise. And I think that's what Democrats are trying to do at this point. They need a big tent. They need to make the big case to Americans that you can -- if you want to keep with all of -- everything that's going on, keep voting Republican.

If you want that to end, give someone else a shot.

David Brooks:

Just one quick thing. I think we lived through the era of what we will call neoliberalism, Clinton, Obama, Bush. That may have died, much as I would lament that fact. But it's been replaced by two successor ideologies, one on the left, which Ibram Kendi, Robin DiAngelo, one on the right, which is MAGA.

I think both those successor ideologies are now in the process of cracking up. And the question would becomes, what's next? How -- is there a new moderate? Is there something else, something? One has a sense of a succession of belief systems that we're now on the end of. And I wish I knew what came next.

William Brangham:

I'd like to pivot to Iran just because it seems -- I know we keep talking about it here on Fridays, but that war does now seem to be in this incredible stalemate, where you have the richest, most powerful military on the planet has been forced into a stalemate by what was already an economically struggling smaller nation.

How do you see this unfolding, Kimberly?

Kimberly Atkins Stohr:

Yes, it's a disaster, not only for Americans in the pocketbooks that -- being hit in the pocketbook every time they go get gas, but also for our military. We have depleted our military arsenal.

You have reports about sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln who are -- the morale is so low, there are reported suicide attempts on it happening on it. And you have family members of those folks who are absolutely gutted and terrified. And you have the president today just dismissing those concerns.

It's beyond a political problem. It's a massive problem. I don't feel safer knowing that Iran no longer fears what the U.S. president says, and they can ignore it, as they have been.

William Brangham:

I mean, the president today -- again, there have been reports that he's going to say, I'm going to declare victory with the Strait of Hormuz and back out. Today, he said maybe I will just declare that the Strait of Hormuz is a piece of American territory.

Obviously, it is a piece of another nation's territory.

David Brooks:

Or no nation's territory.

William Brangham:

How do -- do you think that Trump could actually just -- quote, unquote -- "declare victory" and get out of this?

David Brooks:

Yes, it's -- tell that to a guy driving an oil tanker. He can say whatever he wants, but the raw facts are there was like 130 tankers going through the strait every day before the war. And now that's down to, what, a dozen or so.

So it's -- you just can't argue with reality.

William Brangham:

As much as he tries.

David Brooks:

And it's -- the whole battlefield has shifted against us.

The U.S. forces, in order to keep the strait open, has to protect everything all the time. All Iran has to do is send a drone into one tanker, and no company's going to want to risk their tankers. And so it's all on the -- all the advantage is on their side, and I don't see this ending any time soon.

Finally, I have been reminded this week, two days before Russia invaded Ukraine, I went to the Pentagon, had a senior briefing from a senior figure there, and they said Ukraine's going to lose in five days. Their military is just weak.

Well, we have lived through the 21st century, where the U.S. military, the strongest in the world, has become enemies with a lot of much smaller and weaker militaries, and we have lost every time. So that suggests we're in a different period as we think about military strength. And the Iranians have certainly mastered asymmetric warfare, so we're running out of all our supplies, and we're feeling the domestic effects that Kimberly talked about.

And as I said on this program before, I really think this is going to go on and on and on and on, because nobody -- Iran has no incentive to let the straits go.

William Brangham:

David Brooks, Kimberly Atkins Stohr, so nice to see you both. Thank you.

David Brooks:

Thank you.

Kimberly Atkins Stohr:

Thanks for having us.

title: New Zealand targets outcomes as international education demand accelerates
summary:
As demand spikes and public support holds firm, New Zealand’s international education sector has a crucial chance to show it can deliver real outcomes.

The post New Zealand targets outcomes as international education demand accelerates appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Speaking at The PIE Live Asia Pacific, sector leaders from across universities and institutes of technology and national bodies described a recovery that is smaller in scale than neighbouring Australia’s, but potentially more sustainable.

Marie Clark, director of insights and performance at Education New Zealand (ENZ), reminded delegates that public backing for the sector remains strong.

Referring to ENZ’s social licence research, she noted that last year 77% of New Zealanders see the benefits of international students, and 77% would like to see the same number, or more, international students coming to New Zealand.

Those numbers matter, she suggested, alongside growth indicators and student experience data, as New Zealand works through “what sort of growth as a country we should be aiming for”

New Zealand’s reset is now visible in the numbers. Enrolments rebounded in 2025, with universities and schools together accounting for around 65% of total volume.

Where Australia experienced a rapid post‑border reopening surge, New Zealand’s border stayed closed longer and reopened later, leading to a slower rebuild.

“At Victoria University, we only just recovered our international student numbers this semester – we’re talking about recovery literally last week,” said Amy Rutherford, director international at Victoria University of Wellington.

“That slower recovery, though, I think, has meant that New Zealand doesn’t have the same headwinds that perhaps Australia is facing at the moment in terms of the massive, huge recovery that you had much earlier, which I think perhaps impacted social licence within Australia in a way that we haven’t seen in New Zealand.”

At the same time, structural pressures at home are real, she explained, noting that “government has been quite clear that there will be no more funding for universities”.

“So universities have to seek sources of funding, and international education is a fundamental part of that,” she continued.

Operationally, institutions are dealing with a spike in interest.

“We do have a lot of demand,” she said. “At the moment we are waterboarded with applications.”

At her institution, application volumes are now “about five times what they were two years ago”, but conversion has fallen. Immigration New Zealand used to see roughly half of offer‑holders progress to a visa application, now it is closer to 15-20%.

Dani Mao, employability manager at Otago Polytechnic Auckland International Campus, brought the on‑the‑ground perspective from working daily with international students.

Prospective students – and even those already admitted – are asking very specific, very relevant questions, she explained.

“They’re asking us to list the industry partners we work with, the companies we send interns to, and the outcome of our graduates… how long on average [until] international students are employed, and they even ask about the [salary] range.”

“Some of this information we don’t actually capture well enough, because a lot of graduate outcomes data is based on voluntary surveys,” said Mao.

“We would love to have more information from government and from our own institutional data to be able to give students more information – but the data is hard to crunch.”

Clark agreed that better graduate tracking is critical, particularly as more international students now stay in New Zealand after study.

“We know we can’t track students very well, apart from institutional surveys,” she said. “But increasingly, students are staying on shore in New Zealand, going into work. So we can, and we will be able to get something out of our government data on what’s happening with their graduates when they transfer into the workforce.”

As Mao put it, the goal is “stronger student outcomes and the outcomes properly tracked”.

title: Conquer the First-Day Teaching Anxiety: Tips for a Strong First Impression
summary:
The first day of college teaching could be the most stressful moment ever in the teaching history of novice faculty members. Generally, the first day of teaching is intimidating for both faculty and students. According to Aydin (2021), it is common to experience anxiety on the first day of teaching, especially among newly experienced faculty members. Anxiety emotions […]

The post Conquer the First-Day Teaching Anxiety: Tips for a Strong First Impression appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
The first day of college teaching could be the most stressful moment ever in the teaching history of novice faculty members. Generally, the first day of teaching is intimidating for both faculty and students. According to Aydin (2021), it is common to experience anxiety on the first day of teaching, especially among newly experienced faculty members.

Anxiety emotions are mixtures of conceptualizations such as cognitive, physiological, motivational, and expressive components. In addition to the tendency for perfectionism (Aydin, 2021). According to Gaines et al. (2025), the stressful emotions teachers face on the first day of teaching are strongly related to cognitive appraisal theory. The theory explains that emotions result from individual interpretations and appraisals of events and situations. These emotions reflect on individuals’ actions and thoughts (Gaines et al., 2025).

Novice teachers most commonly experience these specific stressful emotions that might lead to experiencing anxiety on the first day of teaching.

Another reason for the first-day teaching anxiety could lie in imposter syndrome. According to Shekhawat & Kumar (2023), Imposter syndrome is a psychological status characterized by persistent feelings of inadequacy, self-doubt, and not being worthy in that place, despite evidence of competence and accomplishments (Shekhawat & Kumar, 2023).

It is the negative inner self-thoughts that doubt self-credibility and qualifications. It has been reported that 79% of new teachers experience imposter syndrome and societal expectations (Shekhawat & Kumar, 2023). Social expectations lead to fear of facing students’ criticism and judgment. The problem is that these feelings are real and powerful, to the point that they could adversely affect students’ first-day impression.

Therefore, educators should understand the nature of this anxiety, its roots, and how to overcome it. Otherwise, these thoughts would undermine teachers’ self-esteem and self-confidence.

Let Go of Perfection and Focus on Connection

Setting perfection as a main goal in a new teaching experience is not recommended. According to Jossberger et al. (2025), the high level of teaching performance expertise is not rooted in unique, inherent traits; rather, it is a set of skills that grow over time. It is recommended to not expect perfection in the first round of teaching. Instead, focus on building rapport with your students (Haller, 2025).

Building an effective, inclusive classroom community starts on the first day of school by introducing yourself, your name, and how you would like to be called. Students need to feel your enthusiasm for teaching your course as you introduce yourself. Talk about your credibility, activities, hobbies, and favorite sport.

In addition, the first day of teaching is the day to start. Learning the students’ names. Practicing memorizing students’ names is a key to building a good rapport with them (Buddle, 2014). Use whatever tricks you can to memorize your student’s name. Even if an educator could not get it completely right in the first week, students would appreciate your potential and caring.

Consider How Your First Impressions Begins Before Class

In preparing for the first day of teaching, new faculty may consider their outfit selection. Of course, formal attire would generally be the first choice, but consider that there is a strong connection between the instructor’s first-day outfit and students’ perceptions on the first day of school (Oliver et al., 2021) Instructors who wear a highly formal outfit on the first day of teaching are perceived by students as a sign of competence, credibility, and strictness. However, it also conveys a message of decreased warmth, enthusiasm, friendliness, and sympathy (Oliver et al., 2021). Therefore, depending on your preferences, be mindful that your first day outfit also plays a role in students’ expectations and perceptions. If you choose the informal academic outfit, just be careful to keep your teaching tone formal with your students (Oliver et al., 2021).

Prepare Your Classroom Before Students Arrive

I would recommend becoming familiar with classroom arrangements and settings before students enter the classroom, check the technology tools, set your PowerPoint slides ready to launch, and communicate with other colleagues for support in case of hiccups (First Day of Class | Teaching + Learning Lab, 2025).

Use Icebreakers to Build Classroom Community

Be minful of the power of icebreaker activities in reducing anxiety on the first day of school for both students and instructors. The incorporation of icebreaker activities would help foster a class environment conducive to communication (Great Start and High Note Ending – Lansing Community College, 2026). Additionally, it would reflect on the first-day impression as students recognize that their instructor cares about getting to know them. Finally, the use of icebreaker activities would facilitate the formation of friendships among classmates.

There are a variety of icebreaker activities that instructors could use on the first day of class. For example, assigning students into groups of two or four and having them introduce themselves to one another. Alternatively, it could be more creative, like the” Five Fingers” activity, where each student shares with the class more about themselves using their five fingers theme as follows (Great Start and High Note Ending – Lansing Community College, 2026):

Thumb for naming something they are good at.

Pointer for stating a career goal

Middle finger to tell something that makes you happy (could be a favorite snack)

Ring finger to name someone or something special

Pinky to name something that will have your classmate remember you

Make the Syllabus Part of the First-Day Experience

According to (Meyers & Smith, 2024), students’ impression of the first day teaching is strongly related to their interests in the course (Meyers & Smith, 2024). Therefore, on the first day, prepare to use the session time wisely and introduce the course syllabus to students to explain what you expect from students according to syllabus policies. The more time the instructor spends explaining the course objectives, the greater the students’ satisfaction with the first day (Meyers & Smith, 2024). Ensure that each student reads the syllabus and understands the grading system, attendance rules, and the emphasis on class participation. You may implement activities such as a syllable scavenger hunt or low-stakes quizzes to confirm students’ knowledge of the course syllabus (Meyers & Smith, 2024).

Your First Day Is a Starting Point, Not a Finish Line

Stressful thoughts during the preparation for the first day of teaching are common among faculty members, as it is normal to have these doubts and worries (Buddle, 2014). In the meantime, as a novice instructor, you need to demonstrate self confidence in front of your students, especially on the first day of teaching. Seeking support from other colleagues and advisors is recommended. I would also recommend attending the professional teaching workshops that provide a venue for exchanging experiences and expertise to overcome first-day teaching anxiety.

Currently a doctoral candidate in health science at the University of the Pacific, Dr. Hala Salem holds a Bachelor of Dental Surgery (BDS) from Cairo University, Egypt, and an MS in Dental Hygiene from Old Dominion University. She demonstrates a combination of credible academic and clinical backgrounds, with more than 5 years of experience as a dental hygiene clinical instructor at Carrington College, Sacramento, CA. She is an active member of the California Dental Association (CDA) and the American Dental Hygienists’ Association (ADHA). She is dedicated to teaching and passionate about knowledge dissemination.

Dr. Julia VanderMolen is a Professor for the Public Health program at Grand Valley State University and a Visiting Assistant Clinical Professor with the University of the Pacific, School of Health Sciences. Her research examines the benefits of assistive technology for individuals with disabilities in the context of public health. She is an active member of the Disability Section of the American Public Health Association (APHA). Her current research focuses on exploring the health and medical services available to individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities.

title: NTFS 2026: Changing universities means changing relationships
summary: The post NTFS 2026: Changing universities means changing relationships appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
New National Teaching Fellow Dr Syra Shakir, Associate Professor, reflects on leading anti-racist educational change and the lessons transforming higher education has taught her.

Whenever I am invited to speak at universities, there is one question that almost always comes up.

“Where do we start?”

Sometimes the question is about closing awarding gaps. Sometimes it is about decolonising the curriculum, improving belonging, implementing the Race Equality Charter, or responding to increasing political scrutiny around equality, diversity and inclusion. More recently, it has become a question about how we sustain this work during periods of financial uncertainty, politics of division, geopolitical violence and institutional change.

People often expect the answer to be a new framework, a policy, or a checklist.

It never is.

After almost two decades working across teaching, research, leadership and national policy, I have become convinced that meaningful institutional transformation, despite its structural limitations, begins somewhere much simpler, and much harder.

It begins with relationships and care.

Throughout my career I have worked on projects that, on the surface, appear very different. I have co-created curricula alongside students. Developed award-winning digital pedagogies to tackle racism. Led institutional Race Equality Charter work. Evaluated national race equality initiatives. Developed coaching programmes to improve student success. Worked with universities across the UK to understand what enables sustainable change. More recently, I have established international networks connecting scholars and activists committed to anti-racist education and action.

Yet every one of these initiatives has been driven by the same question:

How do we create universities and communities, where everyone feels they belong, feels respected valued and cared for, can flourish, and has the opportunity to succeed?

Students are not beneficiaries, they are partners

One of the greatest lessons I have learned is that some of the most innovative ideas do not come from committees or strategic planning groups. They come from students.

For years, I have worked alongside students as co-creators, not simply participants. Together we have designed curricula, produced films, developed digital learning resources, facilitated workshops, evaluated institutional change and challenged assumptions about who holds knowledge within universities.

Some of our most influential projects, including my becoming anti- racist training and the two films Mind the Gap and Re:Tension (written, directed and produced by my great colleague and comrade Ricardo Barker) were born from listening to students’ and staff lived experiences of navigating higher education. The resources I created, used in conjunction with the films, have since been adopted across multiple universities and organisations, received national recognition and sparked conversations that traditional staff development sessions often struggle to achieve.

The impact has never simply been about producing a resource. It has been about redistributing power. When students become partners in knowledge creation rather than recipients of institutional decisions, universities begin to see themselves differently.

Change happens through conversations, not compliance

Higher education has become increasingly good at producing strategies. We have action plans, key performance indicators, frameworks, dashboards and governance structures. These are all important. They provide accountability and create institutional focus. But they are not transformation.

Real change happens in classrooms and meetings where difficult conversations are welcomed rather than avoided. It happens when peers feel confident to acknowledge that they do not have all the answers. It happens when leaders create psychological safety for honest dialogue instead of expecting perfection.

Some of the most significant moments in my own work have not happened during committee meetings. They have happened after workshops, when someone quietly says: “I’ve never thought about it like that before.”

Those conversations matter because they represent the beginning of learning.

Evidence should help us learn, not simply prove success

Alongside developing educational practice, much of my recent work has focused on evaluation. Evaluation is not about proving that an intervention works.

It is about understanding why it works, for whom, under what circumstances, and how it can be improved.

That shift in thinking is powerful.

Instead of asking whether an initiative has been completed, we begin asking whether it has changed people’s experiences. Instead of measuring activity, we examine impact. Instead of treating equality work as a series of projects, we understand it as a continuous process of institutional learning. The most successful universities I have worked with are not those that have all the answers. They are the ones willing to keep asking better questions.

Courage matters as much as strategy

The landscape for higher education has changed dramatically. Universities are navigating financial pressures, increasing political scrutiny, debates about freedom of speech, artificial intelligence, widening participation, student mental health and rapidly changing expectations of what inclusive education should look like. In this environment it can be tempting to focus only on what is measurable. Yet, some of the most important aspects of higher education remain difficult to quantify.

How safe does a student feel in a seminar?

Does a member of staff believe their voice matters?

Can colleagues challenge institutional norms without fear?

Does someone feel they truly belong?

These questions rarely fit neatly into a spreadsheet, yet they shape almost every educational outcome we care about. Creating environments where these questions can be answered positively requires courage.

Not performative statements.

Not one-off initiatives.

Consistent, intersectional, relational leadership that centres care.

Looking forward

Receiving a National Teaching Fellowship was an incredible honour because it recognised something I have always believed: educational excellence and social justice are not separate ambitions. The best universities do not simply produce graduates. They create communities where learning transforms people, institutions are prepared to transform themselves, and students leave believing they can shape a more equitable society. That work is never finished. Every conversation, every partnership, every piece of research, every evaluation and every classroom interaction offers another opportunity to learn. Perhaps that is the most important lesson of all. Universities are not transformed by policies alone. They are transformed by people who are prepared to listen, learn and lead together.

As higher education continues to evolve, perhaps the most important question is not where we start, but how we ensure that the relationships we build today create institutions that future generations will recognise as genuinely inclusive, courageous and committed to socially just educational excellence.

title: Making universities a part time world
